en: I did not see a wound there.
My Arkesken had gathered rust;
That bitch’s eyes had been blinded then.
Like a spring in the hills,
When we flowed together,
Like a wild ewe and a mountain ram,
When we joined together,
When I laid my arm across his back,
When I drew him close against my breast,
When we were immersed in such delight,
I did not see a wound there.
Such was my king’s lion-like endurance;
Such was the unfortunate woman’s lack of fortune.
The bone of my forehead was sloping.
If my king closes his eyes,
A meager life awaits this unfortunate woman.
I had no hair at the nape of my neck.
If the warrior closes his eyes,
My crown is filled with misery.
My locks were gathered all together.
If the warrior closes his eyes,
My forehead is filled with misery.
On the hills, six san of horses,
O warrior, thoroughbreds and swift steeds mingled,
Driving them along and gathering them in—
Your young son is left behind.
If you truly close your eyes,
Your brothers, elder and younger, are all enemies.
In the mountains, nine san of your horses,
Toburchak steeds and swift horses mingled,
To take possession and say, ‘They are mine,’
Your child, who must gather them, is still too young.
If your mountain-like eyes close,
Your Argyn and Nogoy people are enemies.
My Magnanimous One, if your eyes close,
What will become of this widow?
My sultan, tell your last wishes, speak your words;
Tell this unfortunate woman where she may shelter!
When the moon grows dark,
My king, what shall I do with the night?
Your male heir is left behind, still young.
If your precious eyes close,
My king, what shall I do with the day?
My blue-maned lord, lift your head!
Have you anyone who will look after you?
If your eyes should suddenly close,
My king, have you anyone who will bury you?
Have you anyone who will join what has broken?
Who will grieve like one born in the same nest—
Have you someone close to you?
You have much gold, many gold coins.
O warrior, have you anyone to distribute them?
Your angel of death has drawn near.
Warrior, have you anyone to speak with?
Your winged horse’s head—
Have you anyone who will turn it?
If a dark day falls upon your head,
If a grave and burdensome affair arises,
Without stirring beneath the standard,
Leopard, have you anyone who will stand firm?
If your falcon eyes close,
Unmoving in your service,
Have you anyone who will stand firm?”
Then Manas the leopard said:
“My lady, give me your hand.
If my hour comes and I die,
If you die with me,
Do not settle along the river;
Do not become like an extinguished fire!
Scatter the gold you have gathered and go;
Flee toward your father Temirkan!
If you go to Kara Khan, you will find room;
If you go to Temirkan, you will find shelter.
When a khan dies, his wife’s
Birth family becomes her refuge.
When you go to your father Temirkan,
Semetey in your arms,
That little cradle-child—
Have his foreskin cut,
Perform his customary rites,
Pass him through the dog’s bowl,
Have him step across a sword’s edge,
Cut the hair at his back,
And give him to your kinsman Ismayil.
Without letting him know his father’s story,
Without letting him learn his mother’s story,
Raise your little Semetey.
When he reaches twelve years old,
Dress him underneath in a bulletproof coat;
Then tell him his mother’s and father’s story.
If my ancestral spirit is at hand,
I shall support him on his way.
If my patron accompanies and aids him,
I shall cast an eye upon him.
When my eyes have closed,
This Talas will be no home for you.
Scatter your gathered possessions and go;
Flee toward Bukhara.
Those Abyke and Kobosh, two scoundrels,
Chiybyt and Kochkor, making four,
Ajybai and Kolbai, making six—
Treachery always showed in their eyes.
If they could, these men
Were always bent on tripping me up.
Malice showed within their eyes;
Crookedness ran through their words.
Given the chance, those six slaves
Were always bent on acting against me.
Common iron can never become fine steel;
Those scoundrels raised elsewhere cannot become your people.
Patched-together iron cannot become fine steel;
Such rabid dogs cannot become your people.
Ill intent always showed in their eyes.
Should I become like this, the wretched dogs
Were bent on dividing me from my own.
Malice showed within their eyes;
Crookedness ran through their words.
Given the chance, those six slaves
Were always bent on acting against me.
An honorable person does not hold back;
In this world, senseless dogs cannot unite.
Tomorrow, when my eyes have closed,
Will they not devour your orphaned foal?
Will they not then claim to be equal-born kin?
Your gold will not be worth even charcoal.
When those six scoundrels grow fat, they know no honor.
Your silver will not be worth even iron.
When the wretched slave grows fat, he knows not your grief.
Your silk will not be worth even felt.
Once clothed, the wretched dog knows not your worth.
If I should suddenly die
And you bury me in a known place,
If they join with the six scoundrels—
There are khans whom my hand has struck;
There are people who have suffered humiliation from me;
There are claims I cannot escape;
There are enemies who would shed blood.
To take their revenge upon a corpse,
Let them not open up my grave,
Drag me out onto the road,
And leave me to be torn by dogs.
Be watchful about this!
My fierce one, dig my grave with a mattock.
Without letting a single person know,
Take counsel with Bakai
And lay me in an unknown place.
Heroic woman Kanykei,
Let your courage excel!
Think deeply and wisely about me;
Hide me in a place no one will notice.
When the stars shimmered in the sky—
Let me come to when they stirred;
For myself in the other world,
Let me speak of those who became my friends.
Dwelling in Jetisu,
Everyone who saw him
Called him an accomplished, mighty warrior.
He saddled his leopard
And pecked at the head of Khangai.
He received a blessing from a royal holy man
And was named Koshoi the Leopard.
“To receive a khan’s blessing,” he said,
He studied in Mecca for five years.
Receiving a blessing from the renowned one,
He was named Koshoi the Champion.
His blessing enriched the people
And brought good fortune to those he regarded.
His wide-open eyes were like Venus;
His moon-like ears were like shields.
He joined what had broken,
Gathered what had scattered.
Khan Koshoi of the Katagan
Was a man of complete wisdom,
A khan of true distinction.
He was the one who could find a way.
Send word to Khan Koshoi.
When Koshoi comes, you will bury me.
If you seek counsel from Koshoi,
You will be free to do as you wish.
Dwelling in broad Alai,
Everyone who saw him
Called him a stately warrior.
The youngest of nine sons,
A servant of the one God,
Warrior Toshtuk, son of Eleman,
Had a horse like a whirlwind.
When he descended beneath the earth,
For seven years he saw no sun
And suffered the torment of the underworld.
He swung many spears,
Clashed bodily with champions,
And struck black steel against steel.
Choyunkulak, the Iron Giant—
With him warrior Toshtuk
Fought for two years.
To speak thus of warrior Toshtuk,
He is the backbone of Islam.
If you look upon his outward form,
Khan Toshtuk, born a leopard,
Is the lion of Islam.
If my precious eyes close,
Without allowing the khan’s possessions to be plundered,
He is the support who will defend them.
Without shame or wounded pride toward Toshtuk,
He is the warrior to whom you should turn for counsel.
Without distressing you or wearing out your soul,
If you seek Toshtuk’s counsel,
He is the warrior who will stand by you.
Beneath warrior Toshtuk
Is a horse like Chalkuyruk.
At my funeral when I die,
“I shall stay for sixty days,” he said—
Toshtuk has long since given his written pledge.
He is the support on which to gird yourself.
If your Toshtuk brings his authority to bear,
Without throwing you into distress,
He is the warrior who will care for you.
If you look upon him,
He is the lion favored by his patron.
To Toshtuk, son of Eleman,
My fierce one, send that word.
Dwelling in Maseyil,
Among the people called Oirat,
Summering at Saparbay,
Wintering in broad Turpan,
Khan Saikal, daughter of Khan Karacha—
Her precious hair, broad as a girth,
When she tied it tightly upon her crown,
When the lower village was raided,
Saikal, daughter of Khan Karacha,
When she entered the fray then,
Dust rose where she wheeled about;
Souls departed before her wrath.
Wearing a coat like blue iron,
Riding a horse like Algara,
All the forty companions,
She found how to deal with them on the steep slopes,
From the spur where the mountain ended,
From the level, sloping headland,
From the bank of Kum-Darya,
At the edge of Zhylgynduu,
When the forty warriors, born falcons,
Raided her horses,
Saikal shouted and pursued them.
When she attacked the host,
She speared Bakai from his saddle,
Wreaking havoc;
She speared Chubak from his saddle.
When the renowned maiden Saikal
Raised such an uproar,
They fought without looking back;
The forty champions were left on foot.
When Ulak Khan's Syrgak
Lost his wits,
Crying, ‘Greathearted elder, what now?’
He fled around me.
